name: Scottish Gaelic
notes: Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig). ~57,000 speakers (2011 census). Highlands and Islands of Scotland. PERVASIVE BROAD/SLENDER (leathann/caol) CONSONANT QUALITY: a consonant is slender (palatalised) beside ⟨e i⟩ and broad beside ⟨a o u⟩ ('caol le caol agus leathann le leathann'), and the flanking vowel letter that signals the quality is very often NOT itself pronounced — it is a quality marker, not a nucleus. Both halves are encoded in positional_graphemes: consonants take before_front_vowel/after_front_vowel slender variants, and the marker vowels map to the empty string. Stops are voiceless throughout (⟨b d g⟩ = unaspirated /p t̪ k/, ⟨p t c⟩ = aspirated), and slender velars are palatalised /kʲ kʲʰ/ rather than palatal /c ɟ/. ASPIRATION IS POSITIONAL: Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2021) state that 'in word-initial position, stops are either voiceless unaspirated or voiceless post-aspirated. In word-medial and word-final position, the stop series are either voiceless unaspirated or voiceless pre-aspirated'. Post-aspiration is therefore a word-initial property; a medial or final ⟨p t c⟩ after a vowel preaspirates (GD_PREASP_*), and one standing after another consonant — ⟨rt⟩, ⟨lt⟩, ⟨st⟩, ⟨sp⟩, ⟨sg⟩ — is neither word-initial nor post-vocalic and falls in the plain unaspirated series (GD_UNASPIRATED_AFTER_CONSONANT_*). Preaspiration is written [h] before the coronals and labials and [x]/[ç] before the velars (mac [maxk]), the place-specific Lewis pattern of Oftedal (1956). The velar is the documented exception: it is realised [x] before broad ⟨c⟩ (mac [maxk]) and [ç] before slender ⟨c⟩, following Oftedal (1956), a Lewis source in its own right. Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2021) transcribe every pre-aspiration as a superscript [ʰ] regardless of place (aca [aʰkə], muc [muʰk], boc [pɔʰk]) and describe the Lewis realisation as 'typically a voiceless [h]', adding that it 'can be more [x]-like, especially preceding velar stops in dialects such as Barra'. That sentence names the velar environment as where [x] appears and does not license [h] there, so the place-specific Lewis description in Oftedal governs; the uniform [ʰ] of the Illustration is read as a broad notation, not a competing claim about place. VELARISATION is confined to the laterals and the dental/alveolar nasals — 'the only sounds with actively velarised counterparts are laterals and dental/alveolar nasals' (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021; that sentence stands on a cluster of earlier descriptions — Borgstrøm 1940, Ladefoged et al. 1998, Ternes 2006, Gillies 2009, Bosch 2010 — which are named here as supporting literature and were not fetched or checked page by page) — so no velarised rhotic, sibilant or labial is emitted. SONORANTS: laterals and dental/alveolar nasals hold a three-way velarised/alveolar/palatalised contrast, the rhotics a two-way one. Word-final single ⟨n⟩ is the plain alveolar member (sean 'grandfather' /ʃɛn/, nighean 'daughter' /n̪ʲi.ən/) against ⟨nn⟩ for the velarised and palatalised members (seann /ʃaun̪ˠ/, seinn /ʃəin̪ʲ/). The laterals are NOT predictable from spelling in the same way — the same source gives final single ⟨l⟩ as alveolar in dàil /t̪aːl/ but as velarised in caol /kʰɯːl̪ˠ/ — so ⟨l⟩ keeps all three readings in the lattice. The rhotic contrast is /ɾ/ vs /ɾʲ/ with no velarised member and no trill: 'trills are very rare in contemporary production'; word-initial ⟨r⟩ is the same tap as elsewhere (ràdh /ɾaː/, aran /aɾan/, car /kʰaɾ/). The traditional trill is kept as a second candidate only. ⟨ng⟩ spells /n̪ˠ/ plus /k/, surfacing as [ŋk] with the velar nasal allophone — 'velar and palatal variants of these sounds occur in the context of /k/ and /c/, e.g. long ‘ship’ and taing ‘thanks’'; ⟨ngh⟩ is ⟨n⟩ plus lenited ⟨gh⟩ and earns its own key purely to block the greedy ⟨ng⟩ match (AGENTS.md §2 test 3), not because it is a unit. Svarabhakti — an unwritten epenthetic vowel breaking up a sonorant+consonant cluster (arm 'army' [aɾam], ainm 'name' [anam], balg 'belly' [pal̪ˠak], Alba 'Scotland' [al̪ˠapə]; Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021) — is real but is NOT encoded here. It occurs where 'the consonant preceding the svarabhakti vowel is a sonorant', 'the preceding vowel is short', 'the consonant cluster is non-homorganic', and 'the second consonant is not a pre-aspirated plosive'; unlike Irish, where the epenthetic vowel reduces to a fixed /ə/ (modelled in the ga spec's GA_SVARABHAKTI_* rules), the Gaelic one 'is a copy of the preceding vowel', which this engine's phoneme-triggered rewrite rules cannot express without enumerating a rule per vowel×sonorant×cluster combination. Deferred rather than shipped half-modelled. The word-final ⟨-adh⟩ of verbal nouns and the imperfect is [əɣ], spelled ⟨-eadh⟩ after a slender consonant (turadh 'dry weather' /t̪ʰɯɾəɣ/; Bauer 2011 gives glanadh [gLanəɣ], tilleadh [tʲiLʲəɣ] and bualadh [buəLəɣ] in his own notation, and moladh [mɔLəɣ] devoicing to [mɔLəɣ̥] like every other final ⟨-dh⟩, which parts of the gold write as a final [k]). The slender endings ⟨-idh⟩ ⟨-aidh⟩ and final ⟨-gh⟩ stay silent (chaidh /xai/, tagh /t̪ɤ/): of the 329 wikipron gold rows spelled with those three endings, none ends in [əɣ], against 236 of 286 ⟨-adh⟩ rows and 74 of 86 ⟨-eadh⟩ rows that do. The engine ranks word_final above the after-⟨a⟩ position, so ⟨dh⟩ alone cannot carry both readings; the broad ending is keyed instead as the whole ⟨adh⟩/⟨eadh⟩ multigraph, which the maximal-munch tokenizer takes before the bare ⟨dh⟩ whose word_final silence the slender endings still need. Away from the end of the word the same spellings are a vowel in hiatus with the ⟨dh⟩ silent — adharc /ɤ.ərg/, ladhar /Lɤ.ər/, meadhan /mia.an/ (Bauer 2011) — so ⟨adh⟩ reads [ɤ] and ⟨eadh⟩ reads [ia] outside word-final position. KNOWN DEFECT: the tokenizer's grapheme trie is position-blind, so the multigraph also swallows the ⟨a⟩ of the diphthongs ⟨ia ua⟩ standing before ⟨dh⟩ and hides the broad vowel from the consonant behind it — bliadhna, buadhair, fiadhach, cruadhtan and adhlac lose an offglide or a velarised sonorant. A grapheme key that exists only word-finally would need a positional trie, which the engine has not got. The wikipron gold mixes notational traditions and dialects. Counted over its 3720 distinct words, 244 have at least one variant writing a devoicing ring (U+0325 or U+030A) on ⟨b d ɡ⟩ in the Borgstrøm/Oftedal manner this spec does not use (it follows the aspiration-based analysis above), and 986 carry two or more distinct gold strings. Counted over its 6000 rows, 442 write a velarised rhotic /rˠ/ that none of the sources above recognise for Gaelic, and post-vocalic pre-aspiration before a velar stop is written [x] 212 times, [ʰ] 45 times and [h] 6 times. Refs: Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2021), Bauer (2011), Ó Maolalaigh (2008). Inventory and preaspiration cross-checked against Gillies (2009) and Ó Baoill (2010).

sources.notes: Fetched and read directly (open-access PDF via the author's site). The DOI resolves in CrossRef, which returns this title, both authors, volume 51(2) and pages 261-275; CrossRef gives published-online 2019-08-08 and published-print 2021-08, and Cambridge Core and Glasgow Enlighten both cite the article as 2021. Speaker recorded is from Ness, Isle of Lewis. Source for the consonant inventory (/pʰ p t̪ʰ t̪ tʲʰ tʲ kʰ k/ etc.), the aspiration geometry (post-aspiration word-initial only, preaspiration word-medial and word-final), the Lewis [h] realisation of preaspiration, the statement that only laterals and dental/alveolar nasals are actively velarised, the three-way lateral/nasal and two-way rhotic contrasts with their word-initial, word-medial and word-final example sets, the [ŋk]/[ɲc] realisation of ⟨ng⟩, and the word-initial-stress generalisation. Also states explicitly that orthographic ⟨b d g⟩ show 'very little or no closure voicing even in word-medial stops' (citing Nance & Stuart-Smith 2013), so the contrast is aspiration (/pʰ/ vs /p/) rather than voicing — the analysis this spec follows. Describes svarabhakti as real but it is not encoded here (see notes).

allophone_rules.notes: Preaspiration: Scottish Gaelic preaspirates the aspirated stops ⟨p t c⟩ medially and finally after a stressed vowel — the diagnostic feature that separates Gaelic from Irish (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021; Ó Maolalaigh 2008). The realisation is strongly dialectal (six attested patterns, [xk ht hp] ~ [ʰk ʰt ʰp] ~ none); the central pattern encoded here is [h]+stop for the coronals and labials and [xk]/[çkʲ] for the velars. The velar is the documented exception: it is realised [x] before broad ⟨c⟩ (mac [maxk]) and [ç] before slender ⟨c⟩, following Oftedal (1956), a Lewis source in its own right. Nance & Ó Maolalaigh (2021) transcribe every pre-aspiration as a superscript [ʰ] regardless of place (aca [aʰkə], muc [muʰk], boc [pɔʰk]) and describe the Lewis realisation as 'typically a voiceless [h]', adding that it 'can be more [x]-like, especially preceding velar stops in dialects such as Barra'. That sentence names the velar environment as where [x] appears and does not license [h] there, so the place-specific Lewis description in Oftedal governs; the uniform [ʰ] of the Illustration is read as a broad notation, not a competing claim about place. Conditioned on a preceding vowel, so a word-initial stop keeps its post-aspiration and a post-consonantal one falls unaspirated (GD_UNASPIRATED_AFTER_CONSONANT_*).

stress.notes: Scottish Gaelic stresses the FIRST syllable of the word (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021); unstressed vowels reduce to /ə/.
